title: Jaap close
hook: the Tenth Guru's praise now sits beside Nanak's Japji in your morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole Jaap, and your line, all the names. Did the whole hymn play through once? Today, the last day of our thirty with Jaap Sahib. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Some mornings have a shape you could recognize in the dark. Feet on the cold floor. Water on the face. The kettle. The same mug. In many Sikh homes, the shape has words too, and they come in a fixed order. First a quiet, thoughtful voice, five centuries old. Then a faster one, more than a century younger, with a drumbeat in it. One after the other, every morning, for generations. Thirty days ago you only knew the first. Today: Jaap close.
screen: `A MORNING YOU'D KNOW IN THE DARK.` → `FIRST A QUIET VOICE.` → `THEN A FASTER ONE WITH A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Put the two side by side. Japji is Guru Nanak's, the first Guru. It opens the Guru Granth Sahib, on page one. Jaap is Guru Gobind Singh's, the tenth Guru. It opens the Dasam Granth. Two first pages, two Gurus nearly two centuries apart. Japji begins with Ik Onkar, One, and the Mool Mantar: true Name, creator, without fear, without hatred, timeless, unborn. Jaap begins with no mark, no caste, and then salutes the One as akaal, abhai, ajooni. Same truths, different walk. Japji thinks its way forward, pauri by pauri, asking questions. Jaap marches, name after name, through many meters and languages. Sikhs believe the same light, the same jot, passed from Guru Nanak to each Guru in turn. Saying Japji and then Jaap each morning is a small way of hearing that: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth, and the light in both. Now look back at the road. The morning praise, Jaap Sahib. No mark, no caste. King of kings. Named by deeds. The snake's gait. Akaal, the Timeless. The Merciful. Formless, beyond compare. Ajooni, unborn. The armed One, the protector. Sun of suns. Song of songs. The lamp of beauty. The provider. Gobind. One form, many sights. Ender and sustainer. Karunaa, the house of compassion. Breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter. Abhai. Every land. Beyond the fear of death. Keeping the pace. The last stanza. The amrit bowl. Courage. So many names. The whole Jaap. Tomorrow, the third morning bani, ten verses that begin by your grace.
screen: `JAPJI OPENS ONE GRANTH, JAAP THE OTHER.` · `THE FIRST GURU, THEN THE TENTH.` · `ONE LIGHT, ONE JOT, IN BOTH.` · `THIRTY DAYS OF NAMES.` · then, large: `JAPJI, THEN JAAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add Jaap to your mornings, in whatever size fits. Sit and picture tomorrow morning: where you'll be, what you'll do first. Now picture the place where a few lines of Jaap could go. Maybe a recording while you dress. Maybe the four words, ajai, alai, abhai, abai, at the window. Maybe the full fifteen minutes, if your life allows. Choose one, and promise it gently, for tomorrow only. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Jaap close. Thirty days with the Tenth Guru's morning praise, which now sits beside Guru Nanak's Japji: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.
Your line: japji, then jaap. Tomorrow morning, give a minute to each, in that order, even if it's just one line of each. Day three hundred sixty-one. Jaap, done.

screen: `DAY 361 COUNTS.` → `JAAP SAHIB, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: BY YOUR GRACE.`

howItsDone: In the Sikh morning Nitnem, Japji Sahib is recited first and Jaap Sahib second, followed by the Tav Prasad Savaiye; many Sikhs say all three before or around dawn.

fork.setup: it's morning and you have two banis to say: Guru Nanak's Japji and the Tenth Guru's Jaap. in what order do Sikhs say them?
fork.reveal: the Rehat Maryada lists Japji, then Jaap, then the Tav Prasad Savaiye: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nitnem, the daily rule of prayer, in which Japji comes first and Jaap second.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jaap is a second morning prayer, added after Japji.
what it means: it pairs the Tenth Guru's voice with the first Guru's, the same light heard twice every morning.
what a scholar hears: both banis open their scriptures, and Jaap's akaal, abhai and ajooni restate the Mool Mantar's akaal moorat, nirbhau and ajooni.
